meta.title: Special signals, hazard warning lights and the warning triangle
meta.summary: You will learn when you must give way to vehicles with special signals and how an amber beacon differs from a blue or red one. You will understand when you must switch on the hazard warning lights and at what distance to place the warning triangle.

lesson.h: Blue and red beacons: who has special rights
p: The police, ambulance, fire and other emergency and special services sometimes need to travel very fast. That is why their drivers, when carrying out an urgent official assignment with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon switched on, may deviate from many rules: traffic light signals (Chapter 5), the rules of Chapters 8-18 and the requirements of Annexes 1-3, including signs and road markings ⟦19⟧.
There is one condition: they must ensure road safety. And there is an important exception: they always obey the traffic controller's signals.

lesson.h: When an emergency vehicle gets priority
p: To get priority over others, the driver of an emergency vehicle switches on a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a special audible signal, that is, a siren. Even then, the driver may use this priority only after making sure that others are giving way ⟦20⟧.

If an emergency vehicle is escorting other vehicles, for example a convoy of buses, those vehicles enjoy the same right. An organised convoy is three or more vehicles travelling one behind the other in the same lane with their headlights on, behind a lead vehicle with a flashing blue (or blue and red) beacon. It is prohibited to cross it or to take a place in it ⟦21⟧.
A beacon without a siren gives no priority: on an urgent assignment such a vehicle may deviate from the Rules if it is safe, but you are not obliged to give way to it.
lesson.tip: To get priority, both signals are needed at the same time: the beacon and the siren.

list: A vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren is approaching: give way so that it and the vehicles it is escorting can pass unhindered ⟦22⟧.
A vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon switched on is standing ahead: slow down so that you can stop at once if necessary ⟦23⟧. There may be emergency workers or casualties nearby.
Give way calmly and predictably, without sudden jerks or harsh braking: otherwise you may cause a new accident.

p: An amber (orange or yellow) beacon is switched on ⟦24⟧: during the construction, repair and cleaning of roads and when loading damaged or faulty vehicles; when carrying overweight and oversized loads and dangerous goods, and on the vehicles escorting them; on buses carrying organised groups of children. It is also used by cash-in-transit vehicles, mobile teams of private security companies, mobile transport control posts, vehicles escorting groups of cyclists, flora and fauna protection services, mobile teams of the state revenue authorities and paid parking enforcement.

Such drivers may deviate from the requirements of most signs and road markings, from the rules on positioning on the carriageway ⟦25⟧ and from the prohibitions on motorways ⟦26⟧, provided it is safe and they have made sure they are not impeding anyone (para. 43, as amended on 27.04.2026). The exceptions are signs 2.2, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 3.11-3.14, 3.17.2 and 3.20: these are always obeyed. Other road users must not obstruct such vehicles in their work.
lesson.tip: Under para. 41, you must give way to vehicles with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren. An amber beacon gives no priority: you only need to avoid hindering such a vehicle in its work ⟦27⟧.

lesson.h: Hazard warning lights: when they are mandatory
p: Hazard warning lights (often simply called “hazards”) warn everyone around: be careful, this vehicle may be dangerous. You must switch them on ⟦28⟧:
list: in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited;
when dazzled by headlights (then stop without changing lanes, para. 129);
when towing: on the motor vehicle being towed;
when stopping or parking on unlit sections of road or in poor visibility if the position lamps do not work (if possible, such a vehicle is moved off the road, para. 130);
outside a built-up area, when stopping on the shoulder if it is not wide enough to leave the carriageway completely, or if the width of the shoulder cannot be determined.
lesson.tip: Apart from these cases, switch on the hazard warning lights whenever your vehicle may create a danger for others ⟦29⟧.

p: A forced stop is a halt caused by a technical fault, a hazard from the load being carried, the condition of the driver or a passenger, or an obstruction appearing on the road ⟦30⟧. If it happens where stopping is prohibited, switch on the hazard warning lights, place a warning triangle and take steps to move the vehicle away ⟦31⟧.

Stopping with the hazard warning lights on to buy a coffee or wait for a friend does not count as a forced stop. Where stopping is prohibited, it is a violation, with or without hazard warning lights.
lesson.tip: A warning triangle is required not for every breakdown, but in a road traffic accident, in a place where stopping is prohibited, and where visibility is less than 100 m in at least one direction ⟦32⟧.

p: Flashing lights are sometimes not enough: around a bend or in the dark, they are noticed too late. So in dangerous situations, a warning triangle or a flashing red lamp is also placed ⟦33⟧.

First switch on the hazard warning lights, then immediately place the triangle on the carriageway on the side of greatest danger, usually behind the vehicle. If the hazard warning lights are faulty or missing, place the triangle straight away. In a road traffic accident, these are the first actions; helping casualties and reporting to the police come only after that ⟦34⟧.
list: When it is mandatory: in a road traffic accident; in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited; in a forced stop where visibility of the road is less than 100 m in at least one direction.

At what distance: so that other drivers notice the danger in time in the particular situation, but no closer than 15 m to the vehicle in a built-up area and no closer than 30 m outside a built-up area.
lesson.tip: 15 m in town and 30 m out of town are only the minimum. On a bend or in fog, place the triangle further away so that it is seen in time.

p: If the motor vehicle being towed has no hazard warning lights or they do not work, a warning triangle is fixed to its rear ⟦35⟧. That way, drivers behind immediately understand that they need to take extra care around this vehicle.

keyFacts: On an urgent assignment, vehicles with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon may deviate from Chapter 5, Chapters 8-18 and Annexes 1-3, but not from the traffic controller's signals ⟦1⟧.
To get priority, both a beacon and a siren are needed; the priority may be used only after making sure that others are giving way ⟦2⟧.
You give way to vehicles with a beacon and siren on and to the vehicles they escort ⟦3⟧.
Near a stationary vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon, slow down so that you can stop immediately if necessary ⟦4⟧.
Vehicles with an amber (orange or yellow) beacon must not be obstructed in their work, but they have no priority; they always obey signs 2.2, 2.4-2.6, 3.11-3.14, 3.17.2 and 3.20 ⟦5⟧.
Hazard warning lights are mandatory in a road traffic accident, in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited, when reversing, when dazzled and on a towed vehicle ⟦6⟧.
Outside a built-up area, switch on the hazard warning lights when stopping on the shoulder if it is too narrow to pull off the carriageway completely or its width cannot be determined ⟦7⟧.
A warning triangle is mandatory in a road traffic accident and in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited or visibility is less than 100 m ⟦8⟧.
The warning triangle is placed no closer than 15 m to the vehicle in a built-up area and no closer than 30 m outside a built-up area ⟦9⟧.
Instead of a warning triangle, you may place a flashing red lamp ⟦10⟧.
On a towed vehicle without working hazard warning lights, a warning triangle is fixed at the rear ⟦11⟧.

A forced stop is only one caused by a fault, a hazard from the load, the condition of the driver or a passenger, or an obstruction; hazard warning lights do not allow you to stand where stopping is prohibited ⟦12⟧.
mistakes: Confusing an amber beacon with a blue one. Under para. 41, you must give way to vehicles with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren, but you only need to avoid hindering the work of vehicles with an amber (orange or yellow) beacon ⟦13⟧.
Driving at the same speed past a stationary police car or ambulance with its beacon on. You must slow down so that you can stop at once ⟦14⟧.
Placing the warning triangle right next to the vehicle. The minimum is 15 m in a built-up area and 30 m outside one, and further in poor visibility ⟦15⟧.
Forgetting to switch on the hazard warning lights when reversing. This is one of the mandatory cases ⟦16⟧.
Thinking that an emergency vehicle with its siren on may ignore the traffic controller's signals. Deviating from the traffic controller's signals is not allowed ⟦17⟧.

Thinking that hazard warning lights allow you to stop where stopping is prohibited. They only draw attention to the vehicle, and only a stop caused by a fault, the load, the condition of the driver or a passenger, or an obstruction counts as a forced stop ⟦18⟧.

questions.q: You are driving in town. In the mirror you can see an ambulance approaching from behind with its flashing blue and red beacons and siren on. What should you do?
options: Keep going: you are driving on the main road
Brake sharply right in your lane
Give way so that the ambulance can pass unhindered
Speed up and drive in front of the ambulance, clearing its way
questions.explain: When a vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren switched on is approaching, drivers give way to let it pass unhindered. Do this smoothly and safely.

questions.q: A police car with its beacon and siren on has driven past you. Following it at a short distance are several buses without special signals, which it is escorting. What should you do about the buses?
options: Give way to them too: they are being escorted
Carry on: the buses have no special signals of their own
Give way only to the first bus, then carry on
Overtake the convoy so as not to be held up behind it
questions.explain: Drivers give way not only to vehicles with special signals but also to the vehicles they are escorting. Escorted vehicles enjoy the same priority.

questions.q: There is a police car on the shoulder with its blue beacon on; the siren is off. What should you do as you drive past?
options: Drive past at the same speed, since there is no siren
Slow down so that you can stop immediately if necessary
Stop next to it without fail and wait for instructions
Switch on the hazard warning lights and drive around it in the oncoming lane
questions.explain: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon switched on, the driver slows down so as to be able to stop at once if necessary. There may be people nearby.

questions.q: A snowplough with its amber beacon on is working on the road and moving without keeping to the road markings. What do the Rules require of you?
options: Give way to it just as you would to a vehicle with a blue beacon and siren
Stop and wait until it finishes its work
Sound the horn to demand that it follow the road markings
Do not obstruct its work, although it has no priority
questions.explain: With an amber beacon on, the driver may deviate from most signs, road markings and the rules on positioning on the carriageway, provided it is safe and does not impede anyone. Other road users must not obstruct the driver's work, but they are not obliged to give way to the vehicle as they would to one with a siren.

questions.q: A fire engine with its beacon and siren on is going to a call. The traffic controller at the intersection has raised an arm straight up. What must the driver of the fire engine do?
options: Obey the traffic controller's signal like all other drivers
Go through: an emergency vehicle may ignore the traffic controller's signals
Go through if the intersection is empty
Switch off the siren and drive around the traffic controller
questions.explain: Drivers of emergency and special services on an urgent assignment may deviate from many rules, but not from the traffic controller's signals. An arm raised straight up prohibits movement.

questions.q: You are reversing out of a parking space. Do you need to switch on the hazard warning lights?
options: No, switching on the direction indicator is enough
Only during hours of darkness or in fog
Yes: they are mandatory when reversing
Only if pedestrians are walking behind the car
questions.explain: Reversing is on the list of cases in which the hazard warning lights are switched on. They warn others about a manoeuvre during which the driver's view is worse.

questions.q: At night on a road out of town, an oncoming car dazzles you with its headlights. Which light signal must you switch on?
options: Main-beam headlights in response
Hazard warning lights
Front fog lamps
Left direction indicator
questions.explain: When dazzled by headlights, the driver switches on the hazard warning lights and stops without changing lanes. The hazard warning lights warn drivers behind you that you are in a dangerous situation.

questions.q: Outside a built-up area you get a flat tyre. You stop on the shoulder, but it is narrow, and the car is left partly on the carriageway. Do you need to switch on the hazard warning lights?
options: No: stopping on the shoulder is always permitted
Only if it is already dark or raining
No: switching on the position lamps is enough
Yes: they are mandatory when stopping like this
questions.explain: Outside a built-up area, the hazard warning lights are switched on when stopping on the shoulder if it is not wide enough to leave the carriageway completely. Moreover, this is a forced stop that creates a danger.

questions.q: In town you have had a minor road traffic accident and have switched on the hazard warning lights. What is the minimum distance from the car at which you must place the warning triangle?
options: At least 15 m
At least 5 m
At least 30 m
At least 50 m
questions.explain: In a road traffic accident, the warning triangle is placed immediately. In a built-up area it is placed no closer than 15 m to the vehicle, outside a built-up area no closer than 30 m.

questions.q: Out of town, your car has stalled just after a sharp bend where the road is visible for less than 100 m. The hazard warning lights are on. How should you place the warning triangle?
options: No triangle is needed: the hazard warning lights are enough
Right up against the rear bumper, so that it is sure to be noticed
No closer than 30 m, so that it can be seen from around the bend
No closer than 15 m to the car: that is enough anywhere
questions.explain: In a forced stop at a place where visibility is less than 100 m, the triangle is placed on the side of greatest danger. Outside a built-up area it is placed no closer than 30 m and so that other drivers notice the danger in time.

questions.q: You are driving on the main road. An ambulance with its beacons and siren on is approaching the intersection from the right, along a minor road. Who do you give way to?
options: Only the ambulance
The ambulance and the white car
Nobody
Only the white car
questions.explain: Everyone gives way to a vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren switched on, even drivers on the main road. The white car faces sign 2.4, so it must let you go first.

questions.q: You are driving on the main road. A police car with its beacon on but without a siren is approaching from the right, along a minor road. Who do you give way to?
options: Only the police car
The police car and the white car
Nobody
Only the white car
questions.explain: An emergency vehicle gets priority only when both the beacon and the siren are on. Without a siren, the police car, like the white car, must let you go first because of sign 2.4. But be careful: make sure it is actually giving way.

questions.q: The light is green for you, and you are going straight ahead. A fire engine with its beacons and siren on is approaching the intersection from the right against a red light. Who do you give way to?
options: Only the fire engine
The fire engine and the white car
Only the white car
Nobody: your light is green
questions.explain: An emergency vehicle on an urgent assignment may deviate from traffic light signals, and everyone gives way to a vehicle with beacons and a siren on, even on a green light. The white car is turning left from the opposite direction, so it must let you go first.

questions.q: In what order will an ambulance with its beacons and siren on, a tram and you go through an intersection of roads of equal status?
options: Ambulance, tram, you
Tram, ambulance, you
Ambulance, you, tram
Tram, you, ambulance
questions.explain: The ambulance with its beacons and siren goes first: everyone gives way to it, including the tram. Then the tram: at an intersection of roads of equal status it has priority over trackless vehicles. You are turning left and go last.

questions.q: A police car with its beacons and siren on is leading two buses. You are driving on the main road. Who do you give way to?
options: Only the police car
The police car and the buses
Only the buses
Nobody: you are on the main road
questions.explain: Vehicles escorted by an emergency vehicle enjoy the same priority as the emergency vehicle itself. You must give way to the whole group: both the police car and the buses, even though the buses have no special signals of their own.

questions.q: An ambulance with its beacons on is standing in the oncoming lane, with people next to it. How should you drive past?
options: Keep the same speed: the ambulance is not in your lane
Stop and wait until the ambulance leaves
Sound the horn so that the people move away
Slow down so that you can stop at once
questions.explain: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon switched on, the driver slows down so as to be able to stop immediately if necessary. The rule does not depend on the lane: people near the ambulance may also step onto your side of the road.

questions.q: You are driving in the left lane, and an ambulance with its beacons and siren on is approaching from behind. The right lane is clear. What is the correct thing to do?
options: Brake sharply so that the ambulance can get around you faster
Speed up and drive in front of the ambulance, clearing the way
Carry on: the ambulance can get around you via the oncoming lane
Move smoothly into the right lane in good time to let it pass
questions.explain: You must give way to a vehicle with beacons and a siren on so that it can pass unhindered. The best way is to clear its lane smoothly and in good time. Sharp braking in front of an emergency vehicle itself creates a danger.

questions.q: A road sweeper with its amber beacon on is moving slowly in the left lane. Is its driver breaking the rule that slow-moving vehicles must keep to the right-hand lane?
options: Yes: a slow-moving vehicle must always use the right-hand lane
Yes, if the hazard warning lights are not switched on as well
No: with an amber beacon this is allowed if it is safe
No, but only at night, when there is little traffic
questions.explain: Drivers of vehicles with an amber beacon on may deviate from most signs and road markings and from the rules on positioning on the carriageway ⟦36⟧, provided it is safe and they have made sure they are not impeding anyone. Other road users must not obstruct their work.

questions.q: A road maintenance truck with its amber beacon on is coming out of a minor road. Who will go through the intersection first?
options: The truck: its beacon is on
You, and then the truck
The truck, if it sounds its horn
Whoever reached the intersection first
questions.explain: An amber beacon gives no priority in traffic. A driver with such a beacon may deviate from many signs, but not from sign 2.4 “Give way”. So the truck lets you go first: you are on the main road.

questions.q: A tow truck with its amber beacon on is loading a damaged car right in the zone of a “No stopping” sign. Is it breaking the Rules?
options: Yes: sign 3.27 applies to everyone without exception
No, but only if the hazard warning lights are on
Yes, if the loading takes longer than five minutes
No: with an amber beacon it may deviate from this sign
questions.explain: An amber beacon is switched on, among other cases, when loading damaged vehicles. With it, the driver may deviate from the requirements of most signs, including 3.27, as long as safety is ensured. Other road users must not obstruct the tow truck's work.

questions.q: You have stopped after a road traffic accident. In what order should you switch on the hazard warning lights and place the warning triangle?
options: Place the triangle first, then switch on the hazard warning lights
Switch on the hazard warning lights, then place the triangle at once
Switch on only the hazard warning lights; place the triangle if it gets dark
Place only the triangle and leave the hazard warning lights off
questions.explain: The warning triangle is placed immediately after the hazard warning lights are switched on. The hazard warning lights warn drivers at once, while you go to place the triangle. In a road traffic accident, both signals are needed.

questions.q: In town your engine stalls, and the car comes to a halt in the zone of a “No stopping” sign. The road is straight and visibility is excellent. Do you need to place a warning triangle?
options: No: visibility is good, so the hazard warning lights are quite enough
Yes: stopping is prohibited here, so the triangle is needed
No: a triangle is only needed outside built-up areas
Only if you have to stand there for longer than 5 minutes
questions.explain: A warning triangle is mandatory in a road traffic accident and in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited, even when visibility is excellent. In town it is placed no closer than 15 m to the car. You must also take steps to move the car away from this place.

questions.q: In town your engine stalls, and the car comes to a halt at the right-hand edge where stopping is permitted. The road is straight and visibility is excellent. Is a warning triangle mandatory?
options: Yes: a triangle is needed for any forced stop in town
No: there is no accident or stopping ban, and visibility is good
Yes, but it must be placed no closer than 30 m to the car
No, and you must not switch on the hazard warning lights here
questions.explain: The Rules require a warning triangle in a road traffic accident, in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited, and where visibility of the road is less than 100 m in at least one direction. None of these applies here. Switching on the hazard warning lights will do no harm: they warn of a danger your car may create.

questions.q: A blue car is towing your car on a tow rope. On which of them must the hazard warning lights be switched on?
options: Only on the blue car, which is towing
On both
On neither: dipped headlights are enough
Only on yours, the car being towed
questions.explain: When towing, the hazard warning lights are switched on in the motor vehicle being towed. Drivers behind can see at once that this car is not moving under its own power.

questions.q: You are towing a friend's car on a tow rope. Its hazard warning lights are working. Do you need to fix a warning triangle to it?
options: Yes, at the rear of the towed car in any case
No: only if its hazard warning lights do not work
Yes, but fix it at the rear of your car, the towing one
No, and its hazard warning lights need not be switched on either
questions.explain: A warning triangle is fixed at the rear of the towed vehicle only if it has no hazard warning lights or they are faulty. Here they work, so they are simply switched on in the towed car.

questions.q: At night on an unlit road, your position lamps stop working, and you have to stop at the edge of the carriageway. What should you do?
options: Nothing: on an empty road at night this is not dangerous
Switch on the main-beam headlights so that the car can be seen from afar
Switch on the rear fog lamps and leave the car where it is
Switch on the hazard warning lights and move the car off the road if possible
questions.explain: When stopping or parking on an unlit section with faulty position lamps, you switch on the hazard warning lights. If possible, such a vehicle is moved off the road; if that is impossible, it is marked in accordance with Chapter 7.

questions.q: In winter, out of town, you stop at the edge of the road. The shoulder is covered in snow, and you cannot tell where it ends. Do you need to switch on the hazard warning lights?
options: No: hazard warning lights are not needed when stopping on the shoulder
Only during hours of darkness or in a blizzard
Yes: the width of the shoulder cannot be determined here
No, if the position lamps and dipped headlights are on
questions.explain: Outside a built-up area, when stopping on the shoulder, you switch on the hazard warning lights if the shoulder is not wide enough to leave the carriageway completely or if its width cannot be determined in the conditions. That is exactly what happens under snow.

questions.q: Out of town, your car stalls just after a bend: you can see the road 400 m ahead, but only 60 m behind because of the bend. Do you need to place a warning triangle?
options: No: the road is visible far ahead, and that is enough
No: in a breakdown, the hazard warning lights are enough
Only if it is already dark or fog has come down
Yes: the road behind is visible for less than 100 m
questions.explain: In a forced stop where visibility of the road is less than 100 m in at least one direction, a warning triangle is mandatory. It is placed on the side of greatest danger, here behind the car, so that drivers coming round the bend notice it in time.

questions.q: Out of town, your car is standing on the carriageway after a road traffic accident, with the hazard warning lights on. Where may you place the warning triangle?
options: Only at point A
Only at point B
At either point
At neither point
questions.explain: Outside a built-up area, the triangle is placed no closer than 30 m to the vehicle: point A at 20 m is too close, point B at 40 m is suitable. Both points are behind the car, on the side of approaching traffic.

questions.q: In town, your car is standing on the carriageway after a road traffic accident, with the hazard warning lights on. Where may you place the warning triangle?
options: Only at point A
Only at point B
At either point
At neither point
questions.explain: In a built-up area, the triangle is placed no closer than 15 m to the vehicle, so both points are suitable: both 20 m and 40 m. Choose a place where drivers behind will notice the triangle in time.

questions.q: You are driving on a roundabout. An ambulance with its beacons and siren on is approaching the entry on the right. Who do you give way to?
options: Only the ambulance
The ambulance and the green car
Only the green car
Nobody: you are already on the roundabout
questions.explain: Normally, drivers entering a roundabout with sign 2.4 let those already driving round it go first. But everyone gives way to a vehicle with beacons and a siren on. The green car faces sign 2.4 and lets you go first.

questions.q: What should you do with the warning triangle if the hazard warning lights are faulty and the Rules require a triangle?
options: Place the triangle immediately
Repair the hazard warning lights first, then place the triangle
No triangle is needed, since there are no hazard warning lights
Place the triangle only when it gets dark
questions.explain: The warning triangle (or a flashing red lamp) is placed immediately: after the hazard warning lights are switched on, or straight away if they are faulty or missing. Without hazard warning lights, the triangle is especially important.

questions.q: An ambulance is going to a call with its beacon on but without a siren, and it crosses a solid line to drive around a traffic jam. Is the driver entitled to do this?
options: No: without a siren the driver must obey all the Rules
Yes, if it is safe, but the ambulance has no priority
Yes, and all drivers must give way to it
No: emergency vehicles may never break the road markings
questions.explain: With a flashing blue and (or) red beacon on during an urgent assignment, the driver of an emergency service may deviate from the requirements of Chapters 8-18 and from road markings, provided it is safe. To get priority over others, the driver must also switch on the siren.

questions.q: A road maintenance vehicle with its amber beacon on wants to drive around a section under repair via the oncoming lane, crossing a solid line, but a white car is already approaching close by from the opposite direction. May it perform the manoeuvre now?
options: Yes: with an amber beacon the markings may be ignored
Yes: the white car must give way to it
No: it must let the white car pass first
Yes, if it switches on the hazard warning lights in advance
questions.explain: A driver with an amber beacon may deviate from road markings, but only if it is safe and after making sure that this does not impede anyone. An amber beacon gives no priority, and the white car is not obliged to give way.

questions.q: Which requirements may the driver of an emergency vehicle with a blue beacon on deviate from during an urgent assignment, provided safety is ensured?
options: Most rules and signs, but not the traffic controller's signals
Only speed limits, but not signs or road markings
Any requirements, including the traffic controller's signals
None: the beacon only warns that the vehicle is approaching
questions.explain: Drivers of emergency and special services on an urgent assignment with a beacon on may deviate from the requirements of Chapter 5 (except the traffic controller's signals), Chapters 8-18 and Annexes 1-3, that is, from signs and road markings. There is one condition: they must ensure road safety.

questions.q: An ambulance driver has switched on the beacons and siren. When may the driver make use of the priority?
options: Straight after switching on the siren, without waiting for a reaction
Only on a green traffic light
Only outside built-up areas, where speeds are higher
After making sure that others are giving way
questions.explain: The beacon and siren give priority, but the driver of an emergency vehicle may use it only after making sure that others are giving way. Other drivers may not have heard the siren.

questions.q: What must the driver of an emergency vehicle switch on to get priority over other road users?
options: Only a flashing blue or red beacon
A flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren
Only a siren, without a beacon
The hazard warning lights and main-beam headlights
questions.explain: To get priority, the driver switches on a flashing blue and (or) red beacon and a siren. A beacon alone is not enough for this.

questions.q: Which of these signs must the driver of a vehicle with an amber beacon on obey even while working?
options: 3.27 “No stopping”
3.28 “No parking”
2.4 “Give way”
3.19 “No U-turn”
questions.explain: With an amber beacon, the driver may deviate from most signs and road markings, but not from signs 2.2, 2.4, 2.5, 2.6, 3.11-3.14, 3.17.2 and 3.20. Such vehicles comply with the priority rules, the mass and dimension limits and the ban on overtaking.

questions.q: What colour flashing beacon are buses carrying organised groups of children fitted with?
options: Amber
Blue
Red
Blue and red
questions.explain: Buses carrying organised groups of children are fitted with an amber (yellow) flashing beacon, and “Carriage of children” signs are fitted at the front and rear. The amber beacon warns others but gives no priority in traffic.

questions.q: May you switch on the hazard warning lights in cases that are not on the list in para. 44?
options: No, only in the cases on that list
Yes, to thank a driver who has let you through
Yes, to warn of a danger your car may create
Yes, to allow yourself to stop where it is not permitted
questions.explain: Besides the listed cases, hazard warning lights are also switched on in other situations to warn road users of a danger that your vehicle may create. For example, when braking sharply at the back of a sudden traffic jam on a highway.

questions.q: Under the Rules, what may be placed instead of a warning triangle?
options: Any bright object
The spare wheel
A phone torch switched on
A flashing red lamp
questions.explain: Instead of a warning triangle, you may place a flashing red lamp. Its light must be clearly visible both in the daytime in sunny weather and in poor visibility.

questions.q: In which of these cases does para. 44 not require you to switch on the hazard warning lights?
options: When reversing
When dazzled by headlights
When turning right at an intersection
On a motor vehicle that is being towed
questions.explain: Hazard warning lights are mandatory in a road traffic accident, in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited, when reversing, when dazzled, on a towed vehicle, when stopping on an unlit section with faulty position lamps, and on a narrow shoulder outside a built-up area. For turning, there are direction indicators.

questions.q: In which cases is it mandatory to place a warning triangle?
options: In an accident; in a forced stop where stopping is prohibited or visibility is under 100 m
In any forced stop, and outside built-up areas also whenever you stop on the shoulder
Only in accidents with casualties, and also in any stop during the hours of darkness
When reversing, when dazzled by headlights, and whenever you stop during the night
questions.explain: A warning triangle or a flashing red lamp is mandatory in a road traffic accident and in a forced stop in places where stopping is prohibited or visibility of the road is less than 100 m in at least one direction.

questions.q: On which side of the car is the warning triangle placed?
options: Always in front of the car, so that oncoming drivers can see it
Only on the shoulder, so as not to obstruct traffic
To the side of the car, next to the pavement or shoulder
On the side of greatest danger, on the carriageway
questions.explain: The triangle is placed on the carriageway on the side of greatest danger. This is usually behind the car, where traffic travelling in the same direction comes from. If the car is standing beyond a bend, the triangle is placed so that it can be seen even before the bend.

questions.q: How do your duties differ when a vehicle with blue and red beacons is standing by the road and when it is approaching you with its siren on?
options: They do not: in both cases you must stop at once
You may ignore the stationary one and give way to the moving one
Slow down for the stationary one and give way to the moving one
Give way to the stationary one; the moving one need not be let through
questions.explain: When approaching a stationary vehicle with a flashing blue and (or) red beacon switched on, the driver slows down so as to be able to stop immediately if necessary. You give way to a vehicle that is approaching with a beacon and siren on.
